At a glance

Robotic repair has not been shown to improve pain, complications, recurrence or quality of life over laparoscopic repair; it costs more and usually takes longer (low certainty).

Main caveat: a few small trials with experienced surgeons and short follow-up, underpowered for recurrence and chronic pain; one open-label trial (ROLAIS) found fewer complications with robotic repair [4].

Bottom line
Certainty: Low

Randomised trials show no consistent benefit of robotic over laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair for pain, complications, recurrence, quality of life or return to activity, while robotic repair costs more per case and usually takes longer [1, 2, 3, 6, 9]. The one trial favouring robotic repair (ROLAIS/DIRECT, fewer complications and shorter time) was open-label and single-centre [4, 5]. The trials are underpowered for recurrence and chronic pain, so equivalence on these outcomes cannot be claimed [9].

Few small, mostly single-centre trials with short follow-up; inconsistent operative-time results; imprecise for rare outcomes.

What this means for clinical practice

Default choice

Laparoscopic (TAPP or TEP) repair; robotic repair offers no proven patient benefit and costs more [1, 3, 9].

Who may benefit

The evidence does not identify any patient group; benefits in obese patients and in recurrent or complex hernias are untested in RCTs, and the only trial favouring robotic repair involved highly experienced robotic surgeons [4, 5].

Counselling

Expect similar pain, recovery, complication and recurrence risk with either approach; robotic surgery usually takes longer and costs more, and long-term data are limited [2, 3, 6].

Cost per case

Robotic repair costs roughly USD 595not traced more (Switzerland, rTAPP $3327not traced vs TEP $2732not traced) to USD 1837not traced more (US, robotic $3258not traced vs laparoscopic TAPP $1421not traced) per case [1, 3]; the Italian public-payer model gives an incremental cost of €2,224not traced [12]; Indian costs are not known.

Details

Applicability3The randomised evidence covers mostly elective, uncomplicated, primary unilateral (some bilateral) inguinal hernias in predominantly male adults, operated on by experienced minimally invasive surgeons. ROGER excluded recurrent hernias. The Indian trial enrolled uncomplicated hernias only. There are…
Case mix
The randomised evidence covers mostly elective, uncomplicated, primary unilateral (some bilateral) inguinal hernias in predominantly male adults, operated on by experienced minimally invasive surgeons [1, 3, 4, 6]. ROGER excluded recurrent hernias [3]. The Indian trial enrolled uncomplicated hernias only [6]. There are no dedicated randomised data for obese patients, recurrent or bilateral hernias, or the robotic learning curve [9]. Most trials compared robotic TAPP with laparoscopic TAPP, but ROGER's comparator was laparoscopic TEP and VOLTAIRE used an open-console robot [3, 7].
India and cost
One blinded single-centre RCT from AIIMS, India found no difference in early pain, rescue analgesia, operative time or return to activity [6]. That trial reported no cost data. All cost figures come from the US, Switzerland and an Italian model, all showing higher robotic cost per case [1, 3, 12]. Indian per-case costs, robot acquisition and maintenance costs, and the cost-effectiveness of robotic repair in Indian hospitals are not known from this evidence. The modelled analyses do not capture robot acquisition or learning-curve effects.
Training
The Italian model suggests confining r-TAPP to training programmes [12]. Surgeon workload findings are mixed: frustration was higher with robotic repair in RIVAL [1], while NASA-TLX workload was lower with rTAPP than TEP in ROGER [3] and ergonomic risk was lower in VOLTAIRE [7]. No RCT has assessed the robotic learning curve. ROGER's authors acknowledge that some rTAPP surgeons may not have completed it [3].
What would change this answer4A large multicentre blinded RCT powered for chronic pain and recurrence with at least 2-3 years of follow-up. An independent trial replicating the ROLAIS complication and operative-time advantage with experienced robotic surgeons. RCTs in obese patients and in recurrent or bilateral hernias, and…
  • A large multicentre blinded RCT powered for chronic pain and recurrence with at least 2not traced-3not traced years of follow-up.
  • An independent trial replicating the ROLAIS complication and operative-time advantage with experienced robotic surgeons.
  • RCTs in obese patients and in recurrent or bilateral hernias, and studies of the robotic learning curve.
  • Trial-based cost-effectiveness analyses including robot acquisition and maintenance costs, especially from India or similar health systems.
